title: Ramadan: the new moon
hookLine: the month begins when the crescent is seen or the month is counted

cards: The evening after the twenty-ninth day of the month before Ramadan. Just after sunset, on a hill outside a city, a small group stands facing west with binoculars, squinting where the sun just went down.
In a family group chat, someone keeps asking: is it tomorrow? Has anyone seen it? Somewhere else, a committee is on the phone with people in three countries.
Everyone's looking for the same thing: a thread of light, thinner than a fingernail clipping, low in the sky for a few minutes before it sets.

teach.b: That thread is the hilal, the crescent: the first sliver of the new moon. The Islamic calendar is lunar.
Each month begins with the hilal and lasts twenty-nine or thirty days, which is why Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier every year, as you heard on day six.
The Qur'an, in Surah al-Baqarah, says people ask about the new moons, and answers that they are markers of time for people, and for the pilgrimage. The sky is the calendar.
A hadith in Bukhari gives the rule: fast when you see it, and stop fasting when you see it; and if clouds hide it from you, complete the month as thirty days. Simple on a clear night in Medina.
Harder for Muslims spread across every time zone. So Muslims today follow different approaches, and they're open about it.

Some communities wait for a local sighting, with their own eyes, where they live. Some follow a sighting anywhere in the world, or in a particular country. Some use astronomical calculation to fix the dates ahead of time.
That's why two mosques in the same city sometimes start Ramadan a day apart, and why the group chat is so busy.

teach.h: MY LORD AND YOUR LORD IS ALLAH.
teach.b: There's also a short prayer from the Prophet ﷺ for the moment the crescent is seen, reported in Tirmidhi: asking that the month come with blessing and faith, with safety and with islam, submission to God, and ending, speaking to the moon itself: my Lord and your Lord is Allah.

how: Muslims begin and end Ramadan by the new crescent moon: some communities wait for a local sighting, some follow a sighting elsewhere, and some use astronomical calculation, so start dates can differ by a day.

practice: If you can, step outside or to a window after dark and find the moon: a sliver, a half, a full circle, or not there at all. Wherever it is in its month, it's counting days for someone.
If it's too early, close your eyes and picture that thin crescent low in the west just after sunset. If you pray, you can say the Prophet's words to it: my Lord and your Lord is Allah.

wordCard.voice: Hilal. The crescent of the new moon, the first sliver that begins every Islamic month, and Ramadan. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the crescent of the new moon, which begins every month of the Islamic calendar.

carryVoice: Your line: watch for the crescent. Whenever Ramadan comes for you, this is how it starts. One hundred twenty days in.
